analysis.one_liner: Creates military commissions and internal review tribunals for Guantanamo detainees, replacing federal court challenges.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by a senior Republican committee chairman, the bill drew zero cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have written rules for holding and trying people the military calls 'unprivileged combatants' — terrorism suspects held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. It would replace detainees' access to federal courts with a military appeals system, but it would also give detainees rights they did not then have: a lawyer, a tribunal with a presumption of release unless the government proved they were a threat, and a fresh review every 180 days. It would also require the Pentagon to list every detainee it wants to keep and report on each one to Congress every two months. The bill went to the Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced and never came out.
analysis.who_benefits: Guantanamo detainees gain the most concrete items: counsel at every stage, a tribunal where the government must show by a preponderance of evidence that they are a security threat before detention continues, periodic review every 180 days, criminal trials that are open to the public by default and require unanimous agreement by all three commission members on guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and an express bar on holding U.S. citizens under the Act. The public gains transparency: an unclassified list of who is being held and why, updated every 60 days and sent to Congress, and a nonclassified summary released after each tribunal.

how_it_helps.text: A detainee must be released and repatriated unless a tribunal board finds by a preponderance of the evidence that they are a threat to national security or would take up arms if freed.
Detainees get counsel at every stage, appointed if they cannot afford one, and a classification tribunal no later than 180 days after capture, with a new hearing at least every 180 days.

The Secretary of Defense must produce a complete list of everyone the government wants to keep detained at Guantanamo, with a detailed summary of the evidence, and update it every 60 days with reports to Congress.

A conviction requires all three commission members to agree that the defendant is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, and criminal proceedings are open to the public except where classified information or witness safety requires closure.
A detainee found to be a U.S. citizen cannot be held or tried under the Act.

analysis.who_pays: Detainees give up the right to challenge their detention in any federal court — the bill's findings state that detainees held under it 'may not challenge their detentions in the Federal courts of the United States via the habeas or any other statute.' The Federal Rules of Evidence would not apply to tribunals, the government could prove its case by affidavit, tribunals would be closed to the public and could exclude the detainee when classified information is admitted, the government could win repeated six-month delays of hearings without notice to the detainee or his lawyer, and the Defense Secretary's decision to deny a lawyer a security clearance would be final and unreviewable by any court. The executive branch also loses unilateral control: mandatory lists, reports, and release presumptions replace the status quo's discretion.

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates federal habeas review for Guantanamo detainees, routing all challenges through military-appointed bodies inside the Defense Department, with Supreme Court review only at the Justices' discretion.

Tribunals do not have to follow the Federal Rules of Evidence, may admit anything with 'probative value to a reasonable person,' may hear the government's case entirely by written affidavit, and may exclude the detainee when classified material is considered.

A lawyer's ability to represent a detainee depends on a Defense Department security clearance whose denial is final and cannot be appealed to any court, and the government can postpone hearings repeatedly, six months at a time, in secret without notifying the detainee or counsel.
Detainees may communicate only with their interpreter, their counsel, prison personnel, and others the Secretary of Defense approves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine but uneasy trade. It would have given detainees process they did not have — counsel, a presumption of release, and reviews every six months — and imposed real congressional oversight on a detention system then running largely on the executive's say-so. But the price was cutting detainees off from Article III federal courts permanently and running tribunals under relaxed evidence rules inside the Pentagon, where the same department that detains a person also decides who may defend him and what evidence counts. An honest supporter would call it a step toward legality that still leaves detention outside the ordinary court system; a critic would call it a statute that locks that exclusion in.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the 109th Congress expired in early January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, and the bill's stated findings describe it as Congress's response to a Supreme Court ruling on detainee rights, saying the Act would bar federal-court habeas challenges for detainees held under it.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Armed Services the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill had no cosponsors and never reached the Senate floor before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The executive branch is better off: the status quo of detention policy continued unchanged, with no new requirement to list detainees, justify each detention to Congress every 60 days, or presume release absent proof of a threat. Detainees got neither the bill's process rights nor a floor debate on how they should be held and tried.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The executive and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and floor remarks on June 29, 2006, framing it as Congress's answer to the Supreme Court's detainee-rights rulings.

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — after the bill was referred on its introduction day.

against.name: 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Expired on January 3, 2007, without the bill ever being reported out of committee or debated.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no cosponsors and no recorded floor or committee opposition, so no party split on the bill itself is visible — it simply never moved.

industries.note: The bill would hand the Pentagon statutory authority to run military commissions and keep trying terrorism suspects, but it would also strip the executive's unilateral discretion by requiring detainee lists, 60-day reports to Congress, a release presumption, and reviews every 180 days. Its interest in the bill runs partly with the public's (legitimizing prosecutions) and partly against it (insulating detention from federal courts).
